statement: In one survey of 2,553 young adults in a Southern California school-based cohort (mean age 19; asked once, between June 2018 and October 2019; 75% took part), people who reported vaping THC or hash oil, or dabs, were more likely to report bronchitic symptoms in the past 12 months (daily cough for 3 months in a row, congestion or phlegm, or bronchitis) than people who reported never doing so, after adjustment for age, sex, race and ethnicity, financial status, body mass index, nicotine vaping, cigarette smoking and smoked cannabis: adjusted odds ratios 1.73 (95% CI 1.01 to 2.96) for those whose last cannabis vaping was more than 6 months earlier, 1.63 (1.04 to 2.56) for 6 months to 30 days earlier, 2.79 (1.42 to 5.47) for 1 or 2 days in the past 30 and 2.19 (1.18 to 4.06) for 3 or more days. Wheeze was raised only in the top band (2.27, 1.17 to 4.37), and shortness of breath was not reliably raised after full adjustment. Nicotine vaping on 3 or more days in the past 30 was associated with all three symptoms when only age, sex, race, finances and body mass index were adjusted (odds ratios 1.41 to 1.78) and with none after also adjusting for cannabis vaping and smoking (0.85 to 0.96). Overall 17.5% reported bronchitic symptoms (384 of 2,194), 13.0% wheeze and 20.4% shortness of breath; the paper gives no rates by vaping group (editors' rough calculation from its counts: about 12% to 14% of people who never vaped cannabis against about 23% to 31% of those who vaped it on days in the past 30, depending on how people with missing symptom data are counted). The survey was a single snapshot, so which came first is unknown, and symptoms were self-reported with no lung-function test. It did not record the product, device, source or amount vaped, or tobacco mixed into smoked cannabis, and it ran until October 2019, when the national outbreak of vaping-related lung injury (EVALI) was under way, so it cannot show whether the symptoms were linked to the products involved in it. Odds were raised even in people whose last cannabis vaping was more than 6 months earlier (1.73, against 2.19 to 2.79 for vaping in the past 30 days), which argues for caution about reading the link as an effect of recent vaping and points to residual confounding as a possible explanation. No other study of cannabis vaping and breathing symptoms or lung function was read for this batch, and the authors say longitudinal research is lacking. Funded by the US National Cancer Institute; no conflicts reported.
plain: In one survey of 2,553 young adults in Southern California, those who said they had vaped cannabis (THC or hash oil, or dabs) were more likely to report long-lasting cough, phlegm or bronchitis than those who had never vaped it, even after allowing for nicotine vaping and for smoking cigarettes or cannabis. Wheezing was more common only in people who vaped cannabis on 3 or more days in the last month, and shortness of breath was not clearly more common. Nicotine vaping went with these symptoms until cannabis vaping and smoking were taken into account, and not after that. This was one survey at one point in time, based on what people said, with no breathing test. It did not record what was vaped, how much, or whether tobacco was mixed into joints, and it ran until a national outbreak of vaping-related lung injury in 2019, so it cannot show that vaping caused the symptoms. Even people who had last vaped cannabis more than six months earlier reported more symptoms.
population: 2,553 young adults (mean age 19.3; 58% women; 47% Hispanic) in a Southern California school-based cohort, surveyed once a year after high-school graduation (outcome data for 2,194 to 2,396)
exposure: Self-reported vaping of THC or hash oil in an electronic device, or dabs, by recency and days of use (lifetime but not past 6 months; past 6 months but not past 30 days; 1 or 2 days in the past 30; 3 or more days in the past 30)
comparator: Young adults in the same survey who reported never vaping cannabis (for the nicotine comparison, never vaping nicotine); the full model also adjusts for nicotine vaping, cigarette smoking and smoked cannabis
outcome: Self-reported bronchitic symptoms (daily cough for 3 months in a row, congestion or phlegm, or bronchitis) and wheeze in the previous 12 months, and shortness of breath when hurrying on level ground or walking up a slight hill
magnitude: Bronchitic symptoms, cannabis vaping, full-model adjusted odds ratios against never (95% CI): lifetime but not past 6 months 1.73 (1.01 to 2.96); past 6 months but not past 30 days 1.63 (1.04 to 2.56); 1 or 2 days in the past 30 2.79 (1.42 to 5.47); 3 or more days 2.19 (1.18 to 4.06). Wheeze: 1.12 (0.61 to 2.03), 1.47 (0.92 to 2.35), 1.84 (0.88 to 3.86), 2.27 (1.17 to 4.37). Shortness of breath: 0.90 (0.57 to 1.40), 1.25 (0.86 to 1.84), 1.55 (0.81 to 2.96), 1.41 (0.80 to 2.48). Nicotine vaping on 3 or more days in the past 30, bronchitic symptoms, wheeze, shortness of breath: sociodemographic model 1.78 (1.32 to 2.41), 1.41 (1.01 to 1.96), 1.45 (1.08 to 1.96); full model 0.96 (0.63 to 1.46), 0.85 (0.54 to 1.35), 0.96 (0.64 to 1.42). Absolute: 17.5% (384 of 2,194) bronchitic symptoms, 13.0% (312 of 2,396) wheeze, 20.4% (488 of 2,389) shortness of breath overall; editors' rough calculation for bronchitic symptoms from Table 2 counts: about 12% to 14% in people who never vaped cannabis, about 27% to 31% (1 or 2 days) and 23% to 27% (3 or more days) in those vaping in the past 30 days, depending on how missing symptom data are counted. Editors' note: odds ratios overstate rate ratios when the outcome is this common.

evidence.locator: Abstract; Methods › Analytic Sample, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1
evidence.extracted: 2,553 young adults (mean age 19.3; 57.9% women; 1,188 Hispanic, 47.3% of the 2,510 with race and ethnicity data) from a Southern California school-based cohort answered one survey between June 2018 and October 2019, a year after high-school graduation (75% participation). Outcome data were available for 2,194 (bronchitic symptoms), 2,396 (wheeze) and 2,389 (shortness of breath). Bronchitic symptoms were daily cough for 3 months in a row, congestion or phlegm other than with a cold, and/or bronchitis in the previous 12 months; wheeze in the previous 12 months; shortness of breath when hurrying on level ground or walking up a slight hill.

evidence.locator: Results › Respiratory Health Outcomes and Levels of Nicotine and Cannabis Vaping, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Table 1; Table 2 footnote f
evidence.extracted: Of 2,443 people with cannabis vaping data, 939 (38.4%) reported ever vaping THC or hash oil or dabs (concentrated cannabis): 204 only in their lifetime, 490 in the past 6 months but not the past 30 days, 90 on 1 or 2 days and 155 on 3 or more days in the past 30; 110 people had no cannabis vaping data. 1,095 of 2,553 (42.9%) reported ever vaping nicotine. Smoked cannabis on 3 or more days in the past 30: 20.3%; cigarettes: 3.8%.

evidence.locator: Results › Respiratory Health Outcomes and Levels of Nicotine and Cannabis Vaping, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (total row and cannabis vaping rows)
evidence.extracted: Overall 384 of 2,194 (17.5%) reported bronchitic symptoms, 312 of 2,396 (13.0%) wheeze and 488 of 2,389 (20.4%) shortness of breath. Among the 384 with bronchitic symptoms, 185 (48.2%) had never vaped cannabis; Table 2's percentages are shares of people with each outcome, not rates within each vaping group, so the paper gives no symptom rate by vaping group.

evidence.locator: Table 2 (cannabis vaping rows, bronchitic symptoms column; group sizes in the No./Total column; footnotes b and f)
evidence.extracted: Editors' rough calculation from Table 2 counts, not in the paper (Table 2 gives cases by vaping group and group sizes out of 2,553 but no rates within groups). Bronchitic symptoms among people who never vaped cannabis: 185 of 1,504 (12.3%) if everyone without symptom data is counted as symptom-free, or about 14% (185 of about 1,293) if the 359 people with missing symptom data are spread evenly across groups (86% of each group having data). Vaping on 1 or 2 days in the past 30: 24 of 90 (26.7%) or about 31% (24 of about 77). Vaping on 3 or more days: 36 of 155 (23.2%) or about 27% (36 of about 133). The paper says people who gave no respiratory data were less likely to report never vaping nicotine and smoking cigarettes (supplement table, not read), so even spreading may not hold.

evidence.locator: Table 3 (bronchitic symptoms columns, frequency of vaping cannabis rows); Results › Associations of Nicotine and Cannabis Vaping With Respiratory Health Symptoms, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Bronchitic symptoms and cannabis vaping, full model (adjusted for nicotine vaping, cigarette smoking, smoked cannabis, age, sex, race and ethnicity, financial status, body mass index), adjusted odds ratios against never vaping cannabis: lifetime but not past 6 months 1.73 (95% CI 1.01 to 2.96); past 6 months but not past 30 days 1.63 (1.04 to 2.56); 1 or 2 days in the past 30 2.79 (1.42 to 5.47); 3 or more days 2.19 (1.18 to 4.06). Sociodemographic model only: 1.47 (0.97 to 2.23), 1.44 (1.07 to 1.94), 2.95 (1.75 to 4.98), 2.51 (1.63 to 3.84). The abstract prints different values for the full model; Table 3 is used.

evidence.locator: Table 3 (wheeze columns); Results › Associations of Nicotine and Cannabis Vaping With Respiratory Health Symptoms, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Wheeze and cannabis vaping, full model: 3 or more days in the past 30 2.27 (1.17 to 4.37); other levels not reliably raised (1.12, 0.61 to 2.03; 1.47, 0.92 to 2.35; 1.84, 0.88 to 3.86). Sociodemographic model: 2.13 (1.35 to 3.36) in the top band and 1.47 (1.08 to 2.00) for past 6 months but not past 30 days.

evidence.locator: Table 3 (shortness of breath columns); Results › Associations of Nicotine and Cannabis Vaping With Respiratory Health Symptoms, 4th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Shortness of breath and cannabis vaping: sociodemographic model raised at 3 or more days (1.67, 1.09 to 2.53) and for past 6 months but not past 30 days (1.35, 1.04 to 1.75); in the full model no level was reliably raised (0.90, 0.57 to 1.40; 1.25, 0.86 to 1.84; 1.55, 0.81 to 2.96; 3 or more days 1.41, 0.80 to 2.48).

evidence.locator: Table 3 (frequency of vaping nicotine rows); Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Nicotine vaping on 3 or more days in the past 30, sociodemographic model: bronchitic symptoms 1.78 (1.32 to 2.41), wheeze 1.41 (1.01 to 1.96), shortness of breath 1.45 (1.08 to 1.96); full model 0.96 (0.63 to 1.46), 0.85 (0.54 to 1.35), 0.96 (0.64 to 1.42), with no nicotine vaping level reliably associated with any outcome. The authors say residual confounding by cannabis vaping and by smoking cigarettes or cannabis could partly explain the earlier associations.

Limits and explanations given by the authors: cross-sectional design, so temporality is unknown; a school-based Southern California sample with 75% participation, not nationally representative; the cannabis vaping measure includes dabs; longitudinal research on cannabis vaping and symptoms is lacking; possible reasons for a difference from nicotine vaping (chemicals in THC e-liquids, device and heating differences, tampering with products, deeper or longer puffs) were not measured.

evidence.locator: Table 3 (cannabis vaping rows, bronchitic symptoms, full adjustment); Methods › Measures
evidence.extracted: Editors' reading of Table 3: odds of bronchitic symptoms were raised even in people whose last cannabis vaping was more than 6 months before the survey (1.73, 1.01 to 2.96), against 2.19 to 2.79 for vaping on days in the past 30, so the data show no clear gradient with recency; this argues for caution about an effect of recent vaping and for residual confounding. The Methods describe no product, device, source, additive or amount of cannabis vaping, and no record of tobacco in joints or blunts (the questionnaire is in the eAppendix, which was not read).

evidence.locator: Main text before the Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Figure 1 title
evidence.extracted: Weekly hospital admissions for the national vaping lung injury outbreak (EVALI) peaked at 215 in the week of 15 September 2019, within the period (June 2018 to October 2019) in which this survey was taken; the survey asked about nicotine and about THC or hash oil/dabs vaping but not about specific products or additives, and its Methods describe no question on whether anyone had that injury.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E overall high: confounding high (one time point; coarse five-level bands for the other exposures; tobacco in joints and blunts not recorded); self-reported symptoms from people who also reported the exposure; outcome data missing for 14% (bronchitic symptoms), related to vaping and smoking; the stated multiple-testing correction is not shown.

indirectness.note: Worded for self-reported symptoms in this cohort. Read as a claim about lung disease or lung function, or about other ages and regions, it would be indirect.

imprecision.note: Lower bounds of 1.01 to 1.04 for three of four full-model estimates for bronchitic symptoms; the 1 or 2 day and 3 or more day bands hold 90 and 155 people; most wheeze and breathlessness intervals include 1.

grade.reasoning: Observational and cross-sectional, so it starts low. Risk of bias -1: confounding is high, because one time point and coarse adjustment cannot separate cannabis vaping from other exposures (tobacco in joints and blunts, secondhand smoke, asthma) or from reverse causation, and odds were raised as much in people who last vaped cannabis long before the survey as in people who vaped recently. Imprecision -1: several full-model lower bounds sit at 1.01 to 1.04 and the top bands are small. Not upgraded for a large effect (some odds ratios above 2): the most adjusted model still leaves residual confounding that runs away from the null, there is no clear gradient with recency or frequency, and the lower bounds are close to 1. Not downgraded for indirectness because the claim is worded for self-reported symptoms in this cohort. Rating: very low. Worded as an association, never as an effect of vaping; no longitudinal or lung-function study of cannabis vaping was read for this batch.

verification.flag_note: Section 7 draft for the senior author (decision p-ways-of-taking); findings only. Rests on one cross-sectional survey (Braymiller 2020); the authors say longitudinal research is lacking and none was read; no lung-function study of vaped cannabis was read. The abstract's adjusted odds ratios for bronchitic symptoms differ from Table 3 (Table 3 used). The rough absolute rates are an editors' calculation from Table 2 counts and need the second reader's recomputation. The comparison with smoked cannabis and the lungs belongs to the smoked-lungs claim of reader 73. The paper's supplement (eTable 1, on who lacked respiratory data) was not read. No awaited PDF is needed for this claim.
